Examples: "what guards this statement?", "trace this variable within the function", "why is the pdg_query result empty?", "add a CDG query".

Examples: "How does taint analysis work here?", "Why didn't explain find this flow?", "Add a new sink/source", "Review the interprocedural taint code".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

input.prompt:
In this repository (the "memos" note-taking app, Go backend), I need to find the mechanism by which an outbound HTTP request is sent to a user-configured URL. This is almost certainly a "webhook" feature — memos lets users configure webhook URLs and dispatches events to them.

Please find:
1. The single function that actually performs the outbound HTTP POST/request to the user-configured webhook URL (the convergence point before delivery). Give its exact file path and function name.
2. All the places (functions) that call into this webhook dispatch path — trace upstream to find which higher-level operations trigger webhooks (e.g. CreateMemo, UpdateMemo, DeleteMemo). 
3. Specifically, which gRPC/RPC service handler methods (methods on the API service server, e.g. in a v1 or api package, the ones implementing the proto RPC service) transitively reach this webhook dispatch. RPC handlers are the methods that implement the generated gRPC service interface.

Use grep/ripgrep for "webhook", "Webhook", "Post", "http.Post", "http.Client", "Dispatch", and trace the call chain. Report exact file paths and function names for: the convergence/delivery function, the intermediate dispatch functions, and at least 3-5 RPC handler methods that reach it. Be precise and cite file:line.

content.text:
I have the complete call chain. Here are the findings.

## 1. Convergence / delivery function

**`Post`** — `/bench/home/work/internal/webhook/webhook.go:120`

This is the single point that actually performs the outbound HTTP request. It marshals the payload, builds a `POST` request, optionally signs it (HMAC-SHA256, Standard Webhooks headers), and fires it via the shared SSRF-guarded client at `safeClient.Do(req)` (`webhook.go:152`). Every delivery converges here.

The async wrapper **`PostAsync`** (`webhook.go:184`) only enqueues onto `asyncPostQueue`; four background goroutines started in `init()` (`webhook.go:42-55`) drain that queue and call `Post` (`webhook.go:46`). So even async dispatches converge on `Post`.

## 2. Intermediate dispatch functions

All in `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/memo_service_webhooks.go`:

- **`dispatchMemoRelatedWebhook`** (`:48`) — loads the creator's webhooks via `s.Store.GetUserWebhooks`, builds a payload per hook, and calls `webhook.PostAsync` (`:71`). This is the shared fan-out core.
- **`DispatchMemoCreatedWebhook`** (`:15`) → `dispatchMemoRelatedWebhook(... "memos.memo.created")`
- **`DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook`** (`:20`) → `dispatchMemoRelatedWebhook(... "memos.memo.updated")`
- **`DispatchMemoDeletedWebhook`** (`:25`) → `dispatchMemoRelatedWebhook(... "memos.memo.deleted")`
- **`DispatchMemoCommentCreatedWebhook`** (`:30`) — separate path; loads the *related* memo owner's webhooks and calls `webhook.PostAsync` directly (`:43`).

One additional intermediate helper on the update path:
- **`dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects`** — `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/memo_update_helpers.go:66`; calls `DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook` at `:67`.

## 3. gRPC/RPC service handler methods (on `APIV1Service`) that transitively reach `Post`

All are proto-generated RPC handlers on `*APIV1Service` in `server/router/api/v1/`:

| RPC handler | File:line | Path to webhook |
|---|---|---|
| **`CreateMemo`** | `memo_service.go:70` (call at `:157`) | → `DispatchMemoCreatedWebhook` → `dispatchMemoRelatedWebhook` → `PostAsync` → `Post` |
| **`UpdateMemo`** | `memo_service.go:401` (calls helper at `:513`) | → `dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects` → `DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook` → ... → `Post` |
| **`DeleteMemo`** | `memo_service.go:518` (call at `:562`) | → `DispatchMemoDeletedWebhook` → ... → `Post` |
| **`CreateMemoComment`** | `memo_service_comments.go:20` (call at `:119`) | → `DispatchMemoCommentCreatedWebhook` → `PostAsync` → `Post` |
| **`SetMemoRelations`** | `memo_relation_service.go:16` (call at `:48`) | → `dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects` → `DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook` → ... → `Post` |
| **`SetMemoAttachments`** | `memo_attachment_service.go:16` (call at `:48`) | → `dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects` → `DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook` → ... → `Post` |

That's 6 RPC handlers reaching the dispatch path (2 more than the CreateMemo/UpdateMemo/DeleteMemo trio, because `SetMemoRelations` and `SetMemoAttachments` reuse the "memo updated" side-effect helper, and `CreateMemoComment` uses the distinct comment path).

Note: user-facing webhook CRUD RPCs (e.g. `CreateUserWebhook` in `user_service_webhooks.go`) only store/read config and do **not** reach `Post` — they don't dispatch.
